---
title: "Width and gap"
description: "A figure sets an absolute width and a wider gap."
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
  typst:
    output-file: width-gap-typst.pdf
  docx: default
---

The figure on this page sets an absolute width and a gap of `2em`, twice
the default:

```markdown
![Mean ratings.](ratings.png){#fig-ratings .wrap-left width="2.5in" wrap-gap="2em"}
```

## Result

The figure in this section has a fixed width and a wider gap than the
default. This paragraph comes before it, so it runs the full width of the
text and shows how wide the text is.

![Mean ratings.](../images/ratings.png){#fig-ratings .wrap-left width="2.5in" wrap-gap="2em"}

@fig-ratings is 2.5 inches wide in each of the four formats. An absolute
length does not change with the width of the text, so in a narrow text
column the figure takes a larger share of the line. In HTML, a window at
the [breakpoint](../defaults.qmd#breakpoint) or narrower is the exception:
there the figure takes the full width of the text column.

The gap between the figure and this text is `2em`, twice the default of
`1em`. LaTeX, Typst, and Word convert both values to their own units, and
HTML uses them as written. A percent width,
such as the default 40%, is a share of the text width instead. Use a
percent when the same document renders to pages of different widths, and
an absolute length when the figure must keep its size on every page. After
the text passes the bottom of the figure, each line starts at the left
edge of the text again and runs under the figure, as the end of this
paragraph shows.
